items.headline: Meituan open-sources LongCat-2.0, a 1.6T agentic coding MoE trained end-to-end on Chinese ASICs
items.diff_narrative: Yesterday's open-weight column was the Bridgewater and Thinking Machines Qwen3-235B fine-tune — a narrow financial-judgment result argued on recipe and inference economics. Today swaps in a very different open-weight beat: Meituan released LongCat-2.0 on June 30, a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts with roughly 48B active per token and a native million-token context, published to GitHub and Hugging Face under MIT. The net-new structural claim is the training stack, not the benchmark — the model was built and served on a cluster of more than 50,000 Chinese-made ASICs with no NVIDIA silicon in the loop, and it edges GPT-5.5 on SWE-bench Pro (59.5 to 58.6) while introducing a LongCat Sparse Attention scheme for long-context agentic sessions. It also carries a credibility twist absent from yesterday's slate: the model spent roughly two months as the anonymous "Owl Alpha" checkpoint in OpenRouter's global top three, so developers rated it on merit before the name and country of origin were attached. Where yesterday's story was build-versus-buy on a specialist task, today's sharper signal is that the open-weight frontier is no longer gated on access to American accelerators.

items.headline: Cato AI Labs discloses two CVSS 9.8 zero-click sandbox-escape flaws in Cursor
items.diff_narrative: This continues the agent-tooling RCE thread that yesterday's Flowise Custom-MCP proof-of-concept anchored, but moves the target from a niche low-code agent builder into the mainstream coding IDE. Cato AI Labs disclosed a pair of critical remote-code-execution flaws in Cursor, published July 1: CVE-2026-50548 (CVSS 9.8, a path traversal abusing the optional working_directory parameter) and CVE-2026-50549 (also 9.8, a symlink-resolution fallback), both fixed in Cursor 3.0. The attack pattern is the same content-weaponizes-prompt-injection shape the week has been tracing across Flowise and Langflow, but the fresh and more alarming angle is the surface: this hits the editor developers run against untrusted repositories, web-search results, and MCP servers every day, so a poisoned README, web page, or tool response can drive command execution with no approval prompt. The practical action is immediate — confirm every install is on 3.0 or later, since older builds stay exploitable by default. The through-line hardens from a single-CVE MCP-wiring problem into the broader claim that the tool-execution boundary, not the model, is where agent stacks keep converting attacker-controlled text into shell access.

items.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Enterprise spend caps and opens a HackerOne bounty for Fable 5 cyber-jailbreaks
items.diff_narrative: This advances yesterday's Fable 5 restoration storyline from the fact of the worldwide relaunch into the concrete product and disclosure plumbing that the government arrangement implied. On July 3 Anthropic moved on two fronts: Claude Enterprise gained admin cost-governance controls aimed at runaway agent token bills — organization-, team-, and department-level spend caps, model-level access entitlements, a usage-analytics dashboard with an export and Analytics API, agent-effort controls, and real-time spend alerts, framed explicitly against enterprise "tokenmaxxing" and answering the Gartner warning that coding-agent token spend could rival developer salaries. Second, it launched a formal HackerOne program scoped narrowly to Fable 5 cyber-jailbreak bypasses, turning the co-developed jailbreak risk-scoring scheme flagged yesterday into a structured responsible-disclosure path with an early-draft severity framework built with AWS, Microsoft, and Google. The net-new substance beyond yesterday's restoration-and-classifier framing is that top-model access now ships bundled with both the cost-control tooling enterprises need to scale agents and the concrete disclosure machinery the restoration deal required.

items.headline: Crunchbase's H1 2026 tally puts global venture funding at a record $510B with OpenAI and Anthropic taking 43%
items.diff_narrative: No sector-financing item appeared on yesterday's slate, which touched capital only in passing through the Menlo Ventures $3B raise attached to the Fable 5 story. Today opens a net-new financing thread with hard numbers: Crunchbase's first-half analysis shows global startup investment hit a record $510 billion, already exceeding the $440 billion deployed across all of 2025, split $305 billion in Q1 and $205 billion in Q2 across more than 5,000 startups, with 32 venture-backed companies going public above a $1 billion valuation in Q2 alone. The striking figure is concentration — OpenAI and Anthropic together took $217 billion, or 43% of all venture dollars in the half, meaning two companies absorbed nearly half of global startup funding. It quantifies the same capital-funneling dynamic yesterday only gestured at, landing the week Menlo closed its largest-ever raise on its Anthropic stake and amid reporting that OpenAI floated giving the US government a roughly 5% equity position ahead of a public-market debut. The structural read is that AI is no longer one theme within venture; in H1 2026 it was the majority of it.

items.headline: AI events to plan around — AMD's July 22-23 MI400 reveal remains the nearest catalyst
items.diff_narrative: The events tracker carries over with its lead intact — AMD's Advancing AI 2026 on July 22-23 at Moscone, with the MI400 series and "Helios" rack-scale system expected — and the three sub-tracks largely preserved: chip (Hot Chips August 23-25, AI Infra Summit September 15-17), AI-security (SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit August 11-12 in Half Moon Bay, Black Hat and DEF CON 34's AI Village in early August, OWASP Global AppSec November 5-6), and mainstream dev (GitHub Universe October 28-29, AWS re:Invent November 30 to December 4). Today adds new entries to the calendar that were not listed yesterday: Ai4 2026, billed as the largest gathering of enterprise AI leaders, on August 4-6 in Las Vegas, and the ACM AI Leadership Summit on August 30 to September 2 in Atlanta. The agent-security tie-in updates its anchor to match the day's news — Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series is flagged as directly relevant given the Cursor sandbox-escape CVEs rather than the Flowise exploit — while the two nearest actions stay the July 22 AMD keynote and the August 11-12 AI Risk Summit, both called out as natural venues for secure-accelerator and confidential-inference announcements.
